title: OOP Fundamentals
description: Foundational paradigm of software engineering: classes, objects, memory allocation, constructors, access modifiers, and static scoping.

questions.question: What is OOP?
questions.answer: Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) is a programming paradigm centered around 'objects'—instances of classes that encapsulate data (attributes/state) and behavior (methods). The four core pillars of OOP are Encapsulation, Abstraction, Inheritance, and Polymorphism. OOP promotes code reusability, modularity, and maintainability by modeling software components after real-world domain entities.
questions.logic: Interviewers want to see that you do not just recite definitions; they evaluate whether you understand how OOP contrasts with procedural programming (data and behavior bundled together vs separated) and why enterprises use it to manage complexity in large codebases.

questions.question: Why do we use OOP?
questions.answer: We use OOP because it addresses the critical software engineering challenges of maintainability, modularity, and scalability: 1) Modularity: Code is divided into self-contained objects with clear boundaries. 2) Reusability: Common functionality is inherited or composed across classes. 3) Extensibility: New classes can extend existing ones via polymorphism without modifying tested source code (Open-Closed Principle). 4) Security: Encapsulation hides internal representation and protects data integrity.
questions.logic: The interviewer is checking if you understand OOP from an engineering cost perspective: reducing bug surface area, simplifying debugging, and facilitating parallel feature development across distributed engineering teams.

questions.question: What is a class?
questions.answer: A class is a blueprint or template that defines the state (fields) and behavior (methods) that objects created from it will possess. An object is a concrete, runtime instance of a class that occupies allocated memory on the heap.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Class is logical blueprint, Object is physical instance with state and identity, Class defines methods and variables. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is an object?
questions.answer: A class is a blueprint or template that defines the state (fields) and behavior (methods) that objects created from it will possess. An object is a concrete, runtime instance of a class that occupies allocated memory on the heap.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Class is logical blueprint, Object is physical instance with state and identity, Class defines methods and variables. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: Class vs object?
questions.answer: A class is a blueprint, template, or user-defined data type that specifies the attributes and methods that instances will possess; it occupies no memory at runtime (except for class metadata in the JVM Metaspace). An object is a concrete, runtime instance created from that class blueprint; it is dynamically allocated on the JVM Heap with its own independent state and identity.
questions.logic: The interviewer is testing your memory model understanding: classes are loaded by the ClassLoader into Metaspace, while objects are allocated on the Heap with references stored on thread call stacks.

questions.question: What is a constructor?
questions.answer: A constructor is a special block of code having the exact same name as the class and no return type, invoked automatically to initialize an object when instantiated with 'new'. The main types are Default Constructor (provided automatically if none defined), No-Arg Constructor, and Parameterized Constructor.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Initializes object state at creation, Same name as class, no return type, Default, No-Argument, and Parameterized types. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: Can constructors be overloaded?
questions.answer: Constructors can be overloaded (multiple constructors with different parameter lists within the same class), but they CANNOT be overridden. Overriding requires inheritance, and constructors are not inherited by subclasses because they belong exclusively to the class in which they are declared.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Yes, constructors can be overloaded, No, constructors cannot be overridden, Constructors are not inherited by subclasses. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: Can constructors be inherited?
questions.answer: No, constructors cannot be inherited in Java. Constructors are specific to the class in which they are declared because their purpose is to initialize the state of that exact class. However, a subclass constructor can (and must) invoke a superclass constructor using the `super()` keyword, which defaults to the no-arg `super()` if not explicitly specified.
questions.logic: Trap question! Many freshers confuse 'calling' a parent constructor via super() with 'inheriting' it. Interviewers ask this to test your precise understanding of constructor initialization chaining in the JVM.

questions.question: What is the this keyword?
questions.answer: In Java, `this` is a reference variable that points to the current object instance within an instance method or constructor. It serves three main purposes: 1) Shadowing resolution: Resolving ambiguity between instance fields and parameter names (`this.name = name`). 2) Constructor chaining: Invoking overloaded constructors within the same class (`this(...)`). 3) Passing context: Passing the current object reference to another method or event listener.
questions.logic: Interviewers look for understanding of constructor chaining (`this()`) and the fact that `this` cannot be referenced from static contexts because static methods belong to the class, not an object instance.

questions.question: What is a static variable?
questions.answer: A static variable (class variable) belongs to the class itself rather than to any individual object instance. Only one single copy of a static variable is created and shared across all instances of the class. It is initialized when the class is loaded into memory by the ClassLoader (stored in the Metaspace/Method Area) and persists until the ClassLoader unloads the class.
questions.logic: Interviewers test whether you understand memory allocation: instance variables are created in heap memory every time `new` is called, whereas static variables reside in Metaspace and have a single shared instance.

questions.question: Static method vs instance method?
questions.answer: A static method belongs to the class and is bound at compile-time (static binding). It can be invoked directly via the class name without instantiating an object and can only access static fields and other static methods. An instance method belongs to an object instance and is bound dynamically at runtime (dynamic dispatch via vtable). It has an implicit `this` parameter and can access both instance and static variables.
questions.logic: Trap: Can you override static methods? No, static methods cannot be overridden; if a subclass declares the same static method signature, it is 'method hiding', not dynamic method overriding.

questions.question: What are access modifiers?
questions.answer: Access modifiers in Java are keywords that set the accessibility and scope of classes, constructors, methods, and variables. Java provides four access levels: private, default (package-private), protected, and public.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Control scope and visibility, Enforce encapsulation, Four levels: private, default, protected, public. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: Public vs private vs protected?
questions.answer: Java provides four access modifier levels: 1) `private`: Accessible only within the declaring class (encapsulation). 2) `default` (package-private, no keyword): Accessible only within the same package. 3) `protected`: Accessible within the same package and by subclasses located in other packages. 4) `public`: Accessible from any class across any package in the project.
questions.logic: The interviewer checks if you know the exact package vs subclass boundary for `protected`, especially across different packages, and how `private` enforces the OOP pillar of Encapsulation.

title: Four Pillars of OOP
description: Mastering Encapsulation, Inheritance, Polymorphism, and Abstraction. Understanding dynamic method dispatch and runtime polymorphism.

questions.question: Explain the four pillars of OOP.
questions.answer: The four pillars of OOP are: 1) Encapsulation: Bundling data and methods into a single unit (class) and restricting direct access using private fields with getters/setters. 2) Abstraction: Hiding internal implementation complexities and exposing only essential interfaces (interfaces and abstract classes). 3) Inheritance: Deriving new classes from existing classes to reuse code and model 'is-a' relationships. 4) Polymorphism: The ability of an object or method to take many forms, implemented as compile-time (overloading) or runtime (overriding).
questions.logic: A classic opening technical question. Interviewers want a cohesive, real-world architecture example showing how all four pillars work together in a production system.

questions.question: What is encapsulation, and how do you implement it in Java?
questions.answer: Encapsulation is the practice of bundling fields and the methods that operate on them into a single unit (class) while restricting direct access to the internal state. In Java, it is implemented by declaring fields as private and exposing public getter and setter methods with validation logic.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Private fields for data hiding, Public getters and setters, Controlled access and validation. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is inheritance?
questions.answer: DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) advocates that every piece of knowledge or business logic must have a single, unambiguous representation across a system, eliminating duplicate code via functions, inheritance, or utility modules.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Eliminates duplicate code and logic, Reduces maintenance burden when business rules change, Extracts shared behavior into reusable abstractions. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What are the different types of inheritance?
questions.answer: The main types of inheritance are Single Inheritance (class extends one parent), Multilevel Inheritance (class extends a class which extends another), and Hierarchical Inheritance (multiple classes extend one parent). Java does not support Multiple Inheritance with classes to prevent the diamond ambiguity problem, though it supports it through interfaces.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Single, Multilevel, Hierarchical supported with classes, Multiple inheritance supported via interfaces, Hybrid inheritance possible with interfaces. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: Does Java support multiple inheritance?
questions.answer: Java does not support multiple inheritance with classes to avoid the 'Diamond Problem'—ambiguity when two parent classes provide different implementations of the same method. However, Java supports multiple inheritance of type and behavior through interfaces, and handles default method conflicts with explicit override requirements.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies No multiple inheritance with classes, Prevents Diamond Problem / ambiguity, Supported via multiple interface implementation. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is polymorphism?
questions.answer: Polymorphism means 'many forms' and allows an entity such as a method, operator, or object to behave differently in different contexts. In Java, it is categorized into compile-time polymorphism (method overloading) and runtime polymorphism (method overriding via dynamic method dispatch).
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Ability to take many forms, Compile-time (Static / Overloading), Runtime (Dynamic / Overriding). Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: Compile-time vs runtime polymorphism?
questions.answer: Compile-time polymorphism (Static Polymorphism) is resolved at compile time using method signatures and argument types; it is implemented via Method Overloading and Operator Overloading (in C++). Runtime polymorphism (Dynamic Polymorphism) is resolved at runtime based on the actual object instance type in the heap; it is implemented via Method Overriding and Dynamic Method Dispatch using the virtual method table (vtable).
questions.logic: Interviewers evaluate whether you understand how the compiler emits `invokevirtual` bytecode for runtime polymorphism, deferring target method resolution to runtime pointer dereferencing.

questions.question: Overloading vs overriding?
questions.answer: Method Overloading occurs within the same class when methods share the same name but differ in argument lists (number, type, or order of parameters); return type alone cannot distinguish overloads. Method Overriding occurs across a superclass-subclass inheritance hierarchy where the child class provides a specific implementation of a method that has the exact same name, return type (or covariant return type), and parameters as in the parent class.
questions.logic: Interviewers love asking: 'Can you overload by changing only the return type?' (No, compiler error). 'Can you reduce visibility when overriding?' (No, child cannot have weaker access privilege).

questions.question: Can static methods be overridden?
questions.answer: No, static methods cannot be overridden in Java. When a subclass declares a static method with the exact same signature as a static method in the superclass, it is called Method Hiding, not overriding. Static method calls are resolved at compile time based on the reference variable's declared type, whereas overriding is resolved at runtime based on the object's actual heap type.
questions.logic: A classic trap! The interviewer will present a code snippet where a superclass reference points to a subclass object calling a static method, testing if you realize the superclass static method is invoked.

questions.question: Can private methods be overridden?
questions.answer: No, private methods cannot be overridden. In Java, private methods are not visible outside their declaring class and therefore are not inherited by subclasses. If a subclass defines a method with the same name and parameters, it is a completely independent, new method that has no polymorphic relationship to the parent's private method.
questions.logic: Interviewers check if you understand that overriding requires inheritance visibility; because private methods are invisible to subclasses, polymorphism cannot occur.

questions.question: What is dynamic method dispatch?
questions.answer: Dynamic Method Dispatch is the mechanism by which a call to an overridden method is resolved at runtime rather than compile-time. When an overridden method is called through a superclass reference, the JVM inspects the actual object type in the heap and consults that class's virtual method table (vtable). It looks up the function pointer corresponding to the overridden implementation and executes it.
questions.logic: Interviewers look for understanding of the underlying JVM machinery: vtable (Virtual Method Table) indexing and runtime dispatching via the `invokevirtual` bytecode instruction.

questions.question: Why is encapsulation useful?
questions.answer: Encapsulation protects an object's internal state from unauthorized external mutation, enforces business logic validation rules, and promotes loose coupling: 1) Data Integrity: Setter methods can reject invalid input (e.g., negative balance). 2) Maintainability: Internal representation can change (e.g., changing an array to an ArrayList) without breaking external callers. 3) Read-Only Access: Can expose state via getters while withholding setters.
questions.logic: The interviewer wants to see you connect encapsulation to defensive programming and system stability, rather than just saying 'getters and setters'.

title: Abstraction & Java Concepts
description: Abstract classes, Interface contracts, default/static methods, super/final keywords, and Association vs Aggregation vs Composition.

questions.question: What is abstraction?
questions.answer: Abstraction is the process of exposing only essential features of an object while hiding complex implementation details from the user. In Java, abstraction is achieved using abstract classes (which can have both abstract and concrete methods) and interfaces (which provide complete contract abstraction).
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Focuses on what an object does rather than how, Achieved via abstract classes and interfaces, Reduces cognitive complexity. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface?
questions.answer: An abstract class can contain state (instance variables), constructors, and both abstract and fully implemented methods, and a class can extend only one abstract class. An interface traditionally defines only method contracts and constants, supports multiple inheritance, and from Java 8 onwards can include default and static methods, and from Java 9 private methods.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Abstract class: single inheritance, stateful fields, constructors, Interface: multiple implementation, stateless contract, Interface default/static methods since Java 8. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: Can an abstract class have a constructor?
questions.answer: Yes, an abstract class can have a constructor. Although you cannot instantiate an abstract class directly using the 'new' keyword, its constructor is invoked during the constructor chaining process when an instance of a concrete subclass is created via super().
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Yes, abstract classes can have constructors, Invoked during subclass instantiation via super(), Used to initialize superclass fields and enforce invariants. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: Can an interface contain implemented methods?
questions.answer: Yes, since Java 8, interfaces can contain implemented methods using the 'default' and 'static' keywords. Default methods allow adding new capabilities to existing interfaces without breaking backward compatibility for implementing classes, and static methods provide utility functions scoped to the interface.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Yes, default methods (since Java 8), Static methods with implementations, Private helper methods (since Java 9). Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: Can a Java class implement multiple interfaces?
questions.answer: Yes, a Java class can implement multiple interfaces simultaneously by listing them separated by commas after the implements keyword. This enables multiple inheritance of type and API contracts without the memory complexity of multiple class inheritance.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Yes, using 'implements InterfaceA, InterfaceB', Provides multiple inheritance of behavior/type, If default method names clash, class must explicitly override. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is the difference between this and super?
questions.answer: 'this' is a reference variable in Java that refers to the current class instance, used to resolve variable shadowing or call another constructor in the same class via this(). 'super' is a reference variable used to access immediate parent class members, methods, or invoke the parent constructor via super().
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies this refers to current instance, super refers to immediate parent instance, this() invokes overloaded constructor in same class. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the final keyword?
questions.answer: The 'final' keyword in Java is used to apply immutability or restriction: a final variable cannot have its reference or value reassigned (constant), a final method cannot be overridden by subclasses, and a final class cannot be extended through inheritance.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies final variable = value/reference cannot be reassigned, final method = cannot be overridden, final class = cannot be inherited (e.g., java.lang.String). Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is the difference between final, finally and finalize?
questions.answer: 'final' is an access modifier used to make variables constant, methods non-overridable, and classes non-inheritable. 'finally' is a block in exception handling that executes regardless of whether an exception is thrown or caught, ideal for resource cleanup. 'finalize()' is a deprecated protected method in Object called by the Garbage Collector before reclaiming memory.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies final: keyword/modifier for immutability, finally: block in try-catch for guaranteed cleanup, finalize(): deprecated cleanup method in Object before GC. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: Association vs aggregation vs composition?
questions.answer: All three describe relationships between objects: 1) Association: A general 'has-a' relationship where objects have independent lifecycles (e.g., Teacher and Student). 2) Aggregation: A weak 'has-a' relationship where the child object can exist independently of the parent; parent does not own the lifecycle (e.g., Department and Professors; if department closes, professors still exist). 3) Composition: A strong 'part-of' relationship where the child cannot exist without the parent; parent owns lifecycle (e.g., House and Rooms; if the house is destroyed, rooms cease to exist).
questions.logic: A premier Low-Level Design (LLD) interview question. Interviewers test whether you model object lifecycles properly when drawing UML class diagrams.

questions.question: Inheritance vs composition?
questions.answer: Inheritance ('is-a') binds classes tightly at compile-time, exposing superclass implementation details to subclasses (violating encapsulation, known as the fragile base class problem). Composition ('has-a') bundles references to other objects, delegating behavior at runtime. The fundamental software engineering principle is 'Favor Composition over Inheritance' because composition allows swapping implementations at runtime, avoids combinatorial subclass explosions, and maintains loose coupling.
questions.logic: Interviewers check if you know why deep inheritance hierarchies (>3 levels) become unmaintainable in enterprise codebases and how composition enables design patterns like Strategy and Decorator.

questions.question: Why does Java not support multiple class inheritance?
questions.answer: Java prohibits multiple class inheritance to avoid the Diamond Problem and structural ambiguity: If Class B and Class C both inherit from Class A and override method `execute()`, and Class D inherits from both B and C, which `execute()` should D call? Furthermore, inheriting multiple state fields can cause memory layout conflicts. Java solves this cleanly by allowing multiple interface inheritance (where default method collisions must be explicitly resolved by the developer) while restricting classes to single inheritance.
questions.logic: Interviewers want you to name the 'Diamond Problem' directly and explain how Java allows multiple interface implementation while blocking multiple class state inheritance.

title: SOLID + Advanced OOP
description: Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov, Interface Segregation, Dependency Inversion, immutability, exception handling, and Collections.
studyTopics: Java Collections basics: List, Set, Map

questions.question: What are SOLID principles, and why are they important?
questions.answer: SOLID principles are five design guidelines for maintainable object-oriented software: Single Responsibility Principle, Open/Closed Principle, Liskov Substitution Principle, Interface Segregation Principle, and Dependency Inversion Principle. They ensure code is modular, easily testable, extensible, and resistant to regression bugs.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies S: Single Responsibility (one reason to change), O: Open for extension, Closed for modification, L: Liskov Substitution (subclasses substitutable for base). Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: Explain Single Responsibility Principle.
questions.answer: The Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)—the 'S' in SOLID—states that a class should have one, and only one, reason to change. In other words, a class should encapsulate a single business responsibility. For example, a class that parses user data, persists it to the database, and sends email notifications violates SRP; changes to the email service or database schema would both force modifications to that single class. Splitting it into Parser, Repository, and NotificationService restores SRP.
questions.logic: Interviewers test whether you can recognize bloated 'God classes' in code reviews and decompose them into cohesive single-purpose services.

questions.question: Explain Open/Closed Principle.
questions.answer: The Open/Closed Principle (OCP)—the 'O' in SOLID—states that software entities (classes, modules, functions) should be open for extension, but closed for modification. This means you should be able to introduce new behavior or features without altering existing, tested source code. OCP is achieved primarily through Abstraction, Interfaces, and Polymorphic Strategy patterns: when a new requirement arises, you implement an existing interface rather than adding chained `if-else` or `switch` statements to core logic.
questions.logic: Interviewers look for antipatterns: if adding a new payment method requires editing a 50-line `switch(paymentType)` block in your checkout service, you violated OCP.

questions.question: Explain Liskov Substitution Principle.
questions.answer: The Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)—the 'L' in SOLID—states that objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of a subclass without breaking application correctness or altering expected program behavior. A subclass must fulfill the contract established by its superclass: it must not strengthen preconditions (accept fewer inputs), weaken postconditions (guarantee less output), or throw unexpected exceptions not declared by the parent.
questions.logic: Classic textbook interview example: The Rectangle-Square problem. A Square class inheriting from Rectangle violates LSP if mutating the width also mutates the height, breaking client assertions expecting independent dimensions.

questions.question: Explain Interface Segregation Principle.
questions.answer: The Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)—the 'I' in SOLID—states that no client should be forced to depend on methods it does not use. Large, 'fat' interfaces should be decomposed into smaller, role-specific interfaces. For example, rather than an omnibus `Worker` interface containing `work()`, `eat()`, and `sleep()`, create separate `Workable` and `Feedable` interfaces so that a `Robot` class is not forced to implement empty or throwing `eat()` methods.
questions.logic: Interviewers evaluate if you understand how fat interfaces pollute client code with dummy implementations or `UnsupportedOperationException` stubs.

questions.question: Explain Dependency Inversion Principle.
questions.answer: The Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)—the 'D' in SOLID—states two core rules: 1) High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions (interfaces). 2) Abstractions should not depend on details; details (concrete implementations) should depend on abstractions. DIP decouples business logic from specific databases, messaging queues, or third-party APIs.
questions.logic: Interviewers test whether you understand how DIP reverses the traditional top-down dependency flow: the business domain dictates the interface contract, and technical adapters implement it.

questions.question: What is dependency injection?
questions.answer: The Factory Pattern defines an interface or method for creating an object, but allows subclasses or factory methods to decide which specific concrete class to instantiate, encapsulating object creation logic away from the client.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Encapsulates object instantiation logic, Client depends on interface, not concrete constructor, Follows Open/Closed Principle. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is loose coupling?
questions.answer: A thread-safe Singleton in Java is implemented using the Bill Pugh Holder idiom (static inner helper class) or Double-Checked Locking with a volatile variable: private static volatile Singleton instance; public static Singleton getInstance() { if (instance == null) { synchronized(Singleton.class) { if (instance == null) instance = new Singleton(); } } return instance; }
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Double-Checked Locking with 'volatile' keyword, Bill Pugh Static Inner Class idiom (thread-safe without locks), Enum Singleton (best practice in Effective Java). Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is high cohesion?
questions.answer: High cohesion means that all responsibilities, fields, and methods within a single class, package, or module are closely related and focused on achieving one clear objective. A highly cohesive class is easy to understand, test, and maintain because it does not contain unrelated logic. In contrast, low cohesion results in 'God classes' that mix user validation, email sending, logging, and SQL generation into a single tangled file.
questions.logic: Interviewers pair this with loose coupling: The gold standard of software architecture is 'High Cohesion, Loose Coupling'.

questions.answer: In technical engineering interviews, 'How do you create an immutable class in Java' is analyzed by breaking down its fundamental definition, internal architectural operation, and production trade-offs. You should explain the underlying mechanism, contrast it with alternatives, and provide concrete real-world usage.
questions.logic: Interviewers evaluate structured technical articulation: definition first, internal execution mechanics second, and production trade-offs third.

questions.question: What is the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions?
questions.answer: Checked exceptions (like IOException, SQLException) are subclasses of Exception excluding RuntimeException; they are verified at compile-time and must be caught or declared with throws. Unchecked exceptions (like NullPointerException, ArithmeticException) inherit from RuntimeException or Error; they are checked at runtime and usually represent programming bugs.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Checked: verified at compile-time (IOException), Unchecked: verified at runtime (RuntimeException), Checked forces try-catch or throws clause. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is the difference between throw and throws?
questions.answer: 'throw' is a keyword used inside a method body to explicitly instantiate and trigger a specific exception object. 'throws' is a keyword used in a method signature to declare that this method might pass one or more exceptions up the call stack to the caller.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies throw explicitly triggers an exception inside code, throws declares potential exceptions in method signature, throw is followed by an instance; throws by class names. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: Why override equals() and hashCode() together?
questions.answer: In technical engineering interviews, 'Why override equals() and hashCode() together' is analyzed by breaking down its fundamental definition, internal architectural operation, and production trade-offs. You should explain the underlying mechanism, contrast it with alternatives, and provide concrete real-world usage.
questions.logic: Interviewers evaluate structured technical articulation: definition first, internal execution mechanics second, and production trade-offs third.

questions.question: What is the difference between ArrayList and LinkedList?
questions.answer: ArrayList is backed by a dynamically resizing contiguous array, offering fast O(1) random access by index but slow O(N) element insertions/deletions in the middle due to shifting. LinkedList is backed by a doubly-linked list of nodes, offering O(1) insertions/deletions at the ends but slow O(N) indexed lookups.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies ArrayList: dynamic array, O(1) index access, slower insertions/deletions, LinkedList: doubly linked list, O(1) add/remove at pointers, O(N) access, ArrayList consumes less memory per element than LinkedList node pointers. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: How does HashMap work internally?
questions.answer: HashMap works on the principle of Hashing. It uses an internal array of buckets (Node<K,V>[]). When put(K,V) is called, it computes hash(K) to determine the bucket index. If collisions occur, elements are stored in a linked list; in Java 8+, once a bucket reaches 8 elements (TREEIFY_THRESHOLD) and capacity >= 64, it converts to a Red-Black Tree, reducing lookup from O(N) to O(log N).
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Hashing & bucket array calculation (hash & (n-1)), Collisions handled via separate chaining, Java 8 converts linked list to Red-Black Tree at 8 nodes. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

title: DBMS Fundamentals
description: Relational data structures, Schema vs Instance, Primary, Foreign, Candidate, and Composite Keys, and Referential Integrity.

questions.question: What is DBMS?
questions.answer: A Database Management System (DBMS) is system software that enables users and applications to create, define, query, update, and administer structured collections of data while maintaining data integrity, security, and concurrency controls.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies System software for managing data, Provides CRUD operations, Ensures data integrity and security. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.
questions.codeSnippet:
CREATE TABLE Users (id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, email VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE Orders (id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, user_id INT REFERENCES Users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE);

questions.question: What is the difference between DBMS and RDBMS?
questions.answer: A traditional DBMS stores data as files or hierarchical structures with limited relational enforcement and concurrency. An RDBMS (Relational Database Management System) organizes data into tabular relations (tables) with rows and columns, strictly enforces referential integrity through foreign keys, and guarantees ACID properties.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies DBMS: file-based or flat storage, no relations enforced, RDBMS: tabular structure with primary/foreign keys, RDBMS strictly enforces ACID and Normalization. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is a database schema?
questions.answer: A database schema is the formal structural blueprint or design of a database that defines the tables, columns, data types, relationships, constraints, and views. It is defined during database design and changes rarely.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Structural blueprint of the database, Defines tables, columns, data types, constraints, Physical, Logical, and View schemas. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is a primary key?
questions.answer: A primary key is a column or set of columns that uniquely identifies each record in a database table. It must contain unique values for every row, cannot accept NULL values, and each table can have at most one primary key.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Uniquely identifies each record, Cannot contain NULL values, Only one primary key per table. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is a foreign key?
questions.answer: A foreign key is a column or combination of columns in one table that references the primary key (or unique key) of another table, establishing a link between the two tables and enforcing referential integrity.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Establishes relationship between two tables, References primary/unique key of parent table, Enforces referential integrity. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is the difference between primary key and unique key?
questions.answer: A primary key uniquely identifies rows, strictly forbids NULL values, and a table can have only one primary key. A unique key also enforces distinctness but permits NULL values, and a single table can define multiple unique keys.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Primary key: no NULLs, exactly one per table, Unique key: permits NULLs, multiple allowed per table, Primary key creates clustered index by default; Unique creates non-clustered index. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is a candidate key?
questions.answer: A candidate key is any minimal set of attributes that can uniquely identify a tuple in a table without containing any redundant columns. One candidate key is chosen to become the primary key, while the remaining ones are called alternate keys.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Minimal super key, Capable of being selected as primary key, Contains no redundant attributes. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is a super key?
questions.answer: A super key is any set of one or more attributes that can uniquely identify a row within a table. A super key may include extra redundant columns that are not necessary for uniqueness, whereas a candidate key is a minimal super key.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Superset of candidate key, Guarantees uniqueness of rows, May contain superfluous/redundant columns. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is a composite key?
questions.answer: A composite key is a candidate key or primary key that consists of two or more columns combined together to uniquely identify a record, used when no single column alone contains unique values.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Consists of two or more columns, Combined values guarantee row uniqueness, Common in many-to-many junction/mapping tables. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is referential integrity?
questions.answer: Referential integrity is a database rule ensuring that relationships between tables remain consistent. It dictates that any foreign key value in a child table must match an existing primary key value in the referenced parent table, or else be NULL.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Maintains relationship validity between tables, Foreign key must match valid primary key or NULL, Prevents orphan records via ON DELETE / ON UPDATE cascade or restrict. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What are database constraints?
questions.answer: Database constraints are declarative rules enforced on table columns to maintain data accuracy, reliability, and integrity. Common constraints include NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, CHECK, and DEFAULT.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Rules enforced on columns to ensure data validity, NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, CHECK constraint validates value expressions. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

description: SQL sublanguages (DDL, DML, DQL, DCL, TCL), SELECT clauses, filtering, ordering, NULL handling, and aggregate functions.

questions.question: What is SQL?
questions.answer: SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard declarative programming language used to define, query, manipulate, and control relational database management systems.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Standard language for relational databases, Declarative syntax (specify what, not how), Used across MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.
questions.codeSnippet:
SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) AS total_emp, AVG(salary) AS avg_sal
FROM Employees
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
GROUP BY department_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 3
ORDER BY avg_sal DESC;

questions.question: What is the difference between SQL and MySQL?
questions.answer: SQL is the declarative query language itself; MySQL is a specific open-source Relational Database Management System (RDBMS) software that uses SQL to execute queries and manage data on disk.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies SQL is the standardized language, MySQL is an RDBMS software implementation, SQL is to English as MySQL is to a specific speaker. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is the difference between DELETE, DROP and TRUNCATE?
questions.answer: DELETE is a DML command that removes specific rows matching a WHERE clause, logs each row deletion, and can be rolled back. TRUNCATE is a DDL command that deallocates all table data pages rapidly without logging individual row deletes, resets identity counters, and removes all rows. DROP is a DDL command that deletes the entire table data and its schema definition completely from the database.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies DELETE: DML, row-by-row, WHERE allowed, rollbackable, triggers fire, TRUNCATE: DDL, page deallocation, fast, resets auto-increment, DROP: DDL, destroys table schema and data permanently. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What are DDL, DML, DQL, DCL and TCL?
questions.answer: DDL (Data Definition Language: CREATE, ALTER, DROP), DML (Data Manipulation Language: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE), DQL (Data Query Language: SELECT), DCL (Data Control Language: GRANT, REVOKE), and TCL (Transaction Control Language: COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT).
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies DDL modifies structure (schema), DML modifies table data, DQL retrieves data (SELECT). Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is a SELECT statement?
questions.answer: In technical engineering interviews, 'What is a SELECT statement' is analyzed by breaking down its fundamental definition, internal architectural operation, and production trade-offs. You should explain the underlying mechanism, contrast it with alternatives, and provide concrete real-world usage.

questions.question: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
questions.answer: WHERE filters individual rows before any grouping or aggregation takes place and cannot be used with aggregate functions (like COUNT, SUM). HAVING filters groups of rows after GROUP BY has aggregated them and can evaluate conditions on aggregate functions.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies WHERE filters rows before aggregation, HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY, HAVING works on aggregate functions (e.g., HAVING COUNT(*) > 5). Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is DISTINCT?
questions.answer: In technical engineering interviews, 'What is DISTINCT' is analyzed by breaking down its fundamental definition, internal architectural operation, and production trade-offs. You should explain the underlying mechanism, contrast it with alternatives, and provide concrete real-world usage.
questions.logic: Interviewers evaluate structured technical articulation: definition first, internal execution mechanics second, and production trade-offs third.
questions.codeSnippet: // Architectural principle for What is DISTINCT

questions.question: What is the difference between GROUP BY and ORDER BY?
questions.answer: GROUP BY summarizes rows with identical values in specified columns into aggregate summary rows (e.g., total sales per department). ORDER BY simply sorts the final result set in ascending (ASC) or descending (DESC) order without grouping or collapsing rows.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies GROUP BY groups identical rows for aggregate functions, ORDER BY sorts the returned output rows, GROUP BY executes before ORDER BY in query execution order. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What are aggregate functions in SQL?
questions.answer: Aggregate functions perform calculations on a set of column values across multiple rows and return a single summary value. The standard aggregate functions in SQL are COUNT(), SUM(), AVG(), MIN(), and MAX().
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Calculates single summary value over multiple rows, COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX, Ignores NULL values (except COUNT(*)). Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is the difference between COUNT(*) and COUNT(column)?
questions.answer: COUNT(*) counts the total number of rows in the table or result set, including rows with NULL values and duplicate values. COUNT(column_name) counts only the rows where the specified column contains a non-NULL value.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies COUNT(*) counts all rows regardless of NULLs, COUNT(column) counts only rows where column IS NOT NULL, COUNT(*) is often optimized by database engines. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is NULL in a database?
questions.answer: NULL in a database represents missing, unknown, unassigned, or inapplicable data. It is not equivalent to zero, an empty string, or whitespace, and comparisons involving NULL require special operators like IS NULL or IS NOT NULL.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Represents missing or unknown data, Not equal to zero or empty string, Evaluates to UNKNOWN in three-valued logic. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: How do you handle NULL values in SQL?
questions.answer: NULL values cannot be compared using '=' or '!='; instead, SQL provides IS NULL and IS NOT NULL. Functions like COALESCE(col, default_val), IFNULL(col, val) in MySQL, or NVL() in Oracle are used to substitute fallback values for NULLs.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Compare with IS NULL / IS NOT NULL, never = NULL, COALESCE(val1, val2, ...) returns first non-null argument, NULL propagates in arithmetic resulting in NULL. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is the difference between IN and BETWEEN?
questions.answer: IN checks if an attribute matches any discrete item from a specified set of values (e.g., WHERE id IN (1, 5, 9)). BETWEEN checks if a value falls within an inclusive continuous range (e.g., WHERE age BETWEEN 20 AND 30).
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies IN tests membership in discrete set, BETWEEN tests value in inclusive continuous range (>= and <=). Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is a JOIN?
questions.answer: In technical engineering interviews, 'What is a JOIN' is analyzed by breaking down its fundamental definition, internal architectural operation, and production trade-offs. questions.question: What is the difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN?
questions.answer: INNER JOIN returns only the rows that have matching values in both joined tables. LEFT JOIN (or LEFT OUTER JOIN) returns all rows from the left table, plus matched rows from the right table; if no match exists, NULLs are returned for right table columns.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies INNER JOIN: intersection (matching records in both), LEFT JOIN: all left records + matching right records (or NULL), Left rows are preserved even with zero right matches. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is the difference between LEFT JOIN and RIGHT JOIN?
questions.answer: LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table and matched rows from the right table. RIGHT JOIN returns all rows from the right table and matched rows from the left table; right joins are rarely used in practice because swapping table positions in a LEFT JOIN produces the identical result.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies LEFT JOIN preserves all left table records, RIGHT JOIN preserves all right table records, Any RIGHT JOIN can be rewritten as a LEFT JOIN. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is FULL OUTER JOIN?
questions.answer: A FULL OUTER JOIN returns all rows when there is a match in either the left or right table. If a row in the left table has no match in the right table, right columns show NULL; if a right row has no match in the left table, left columns show NULL.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Combines results of LEFT JOIN and RIGHT JOIN, Returns all rows from both tables, Missing matches populated with NULLs. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is SELF JOIN?
questions.answer: A SELF JOIN is a regular join in which a table is joined with itself using distinct table aliases, useful for querying hierarchical or comparative data stored in a single table, such as finding an employee and their corresponding manager.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Table joined with itself, Requires distinct table aliases (e.g., e1, e2), Ideal for parent-child hierarchies like Employees and Managers. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is CROSS JOIN?
questions.answer: A CROSS JOIN produces the Cartesian product of two tables, returning every possible combination of rows where each row from the first table is paired with every row from the second table (resulting in M * N rows).
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Produces Cartesian product (M * N rows), No ON join condition required, Used for generating combinations or matrix schedules. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
questions.answer: WHERE filters individual rows before any grouping or aggregation takes place and cannot be used with aggregate functions (like COUNT, SUM). HAVING filters groups of rows after GROUP BY has aggregated them and can evaluate conditions on aggregate functions.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies WHERE filters rows before aggregation, HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY, HAVING works on aggregate functions (e.g., HAVING COUNT(*) > 5). Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is the difference between UNION and UNION ALL?
questions.answer: UNION combines the result sets of two or more SELECT queries and automatically removes duplicate rows from the final output. UNION ALL combines the result sets and retains all duplicate rows, executing much faster because it avoids an expensive sort/distinct operation.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies UNION removes duplicate rows (slower due to sorting/deduping), UNION ALL keeps all duplicates (faster), Both require matching number and data types of columns. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

title: Advanced SQL
description: Subqueries, Correlated subqueries, EXISTS vs IN, Common Table Expressions (CTEs), and Window Functions (ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK).

questions.question: What is a subquery in SQL?
questions.answer: In technical engineering interviews, 'What is a subquery in SQL' is analyzed by breaking down its fundamental definition, internal architectural operation, and production trade-offs. You should explain the underlying mechanism, contrast it with alternatives, and provide concrete real-world usage.
questions.logic: Interviewers evaluate structured technical articulation: definition first, internal execution mechanics second, and production trade-offs third.
questions.codeSnippet: // Architectural principle for What is a subquery in SQL

questions.question: What is a correlated subquery?
questions.answer: A correlated subquery is an inner query that references columns from the outer query. Because it depends on the outer row, the inner query must be re-evaluated repeatedly for every row processed by the outer query, making it potentially slower than an independent subquery.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Subquery references outer query columns, Executes once per outer row, Evaluated row-by-row (can be computationally expensive). Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is the difference between JOIN and subquery?
questions.answer: A JOIN combines columns from two or more tables into a single result set based on a related column, generally optimized well by query optimizers using hash or merge joins. A subquery is a nested SELECT query inside an outer query, often used for filtering, calculations, or existence checks.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies JOINs combine tables side-by-side into wider rows, Subqueries nest queries inside WHERE/FROM/SELECT, JOINs are usually faster than correlated subqueries. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is a Common Table Expression (CTE)?
questions.answer: A Common Table Expression (CTE) is a temporary named result set defined using the WITH clause that exists only within the execution scope of a single SQL statement (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE), improving readability and modularity over complex nested subqueries.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Defined using WITH cte_name AS (...), Temporary named query scope, Improves SQL readability and maintenance. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What are window functions in SQL?
questions.answer: Window functions perform calculations across a set of table rows related to the current row (a window defined by the OVER clause) without collapsing rows into a single summary output like GROUP BY does, retaining individual row identities.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Calculations across row sets without collapsing rows, Uses OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...), Examples: ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), DENSE_RANK(), LAG(), LEAD(). Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is the difference between ROW_NUMBER(), RANK() and DENSE_RANK()?
questions.answer: ROW_NUMBER() assigns a unique, consecutive sequential integer to each row starting at 1. RANK() assigns identical ranks to ties and skips subsequent rank numbers (e.g., 1, 2, 2, 4). DENSE_RANK() assigns identical ranks to ties without skipping subsequent numbers (e.g., 1, 2, 2, 3).
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies ROW_NUMBER: unique sequential integer, no ties (1, 2, 3, 4), RANK: ties get same rank, skips ranks (1, 2, 2, 4), DENSE_RANK: ties get same rank, no gaps (1, 2, 2, 3). Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is the purpose of PARTITION BY?
questions.answer: The PARTITION BY clause is used inside the OVER() clause of a window function to divide the query result set into separate partitions or subsets. The window function calculation is then applied independently within each partition and resets when moving to the next.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Divides result set into partitions for window functions, Window function resets calculation for each partition, Analogous to GROUP BY but preserves individual rows. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is the difference between IN and EXISTS?
questions.answer: IN checks whether a value matches any value in a specified list or single-column subquery. EXISTS checks for the existence of any matching rows in a subquery and returns TRUE as soon as the first matching row is found (short-circuiting), making EXISTS significantly faster for large subqueries and safe against NULLs.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies IN checks value against list of values, EXISTS checks boolean row existence (short-circuits), EXISTS handles NULL subquery results cleanly. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is CASE WHEN in SQL?
questions.answer: CASE WHEN is SQL's conditional logic construct that evaluates expressions in sequence and returns a corresponding value when a condition is met, functioning like an if-else statement in queries (e.g., CASE WHEN score >= 90 THEN 'A' ELSE 'B' END).
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Conditional if-then-else logic in SQL, Syntax: CASE WHEN cond THEN val ... ELSE default END, Can be used in SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, and aggregates. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: How do you find the top three salaries in each department?
questions.answer: To find top 3 salaries in each department: SELECT department_id, name, salary FROM (SELECT department_id, name, salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) as rnk FROM Employee) t WHERE rnk <= 3;
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies DENSE_RANK() window function, PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC, Filter WHERE rnk <= 3 in outer query. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: How do you find the second-highest salary in a table?
questions.answer: The second-highest salary can be found using: SELECT MAX(salary) FROM Employee WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM Employee); or using DENSE_RANK(): SELECT salary FROM (SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) as rnk FROM Employee) t WHERE rnk = 2 LIMIT 1;
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Subquery with MAX: WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX...), Window function: DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) = 2, DENSE_RANK handles ties properly. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: How do you find the third-highest salary in a table?
questions.answer: The third-highest salary can be found using DENSE_RANK(): SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM (SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk FROM Employee) t WHERE rnk = 3; or with OFFSET: SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM Employee ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 2;
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies DENSE_RANK() = 3 handles ties correctly, ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 2, DISTINCT ensures distinct values. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: How do you find the Nth-highest salary?
questions.answer: To find the Nth-highest salary dynamically: SELECT salary FROM (SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) as rnk FROM Employee) ranked WHERE rnk = N LIMIT 1; or in MySQL: SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM Employee ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET (N-1);
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Window function DENSE_RANK() = N, LIMIT 1 OFFSET (N - 1), DENSE_RANK is standard and handles duplicate salaries. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is database normalization?
questions.answer: Database normalization is the systematic technique of organizing table columns and relationships to minimize data redundancy and eliminate undesirable update, insertion, and deletion anomalies while maintaining data integrity.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Reduces data redundancy, Eliminates insert, update, delete anomalies, Divides large tables into smaller related tables. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: Why is normalization required?
questions.answer: Normalization is required to prevent data duplication, conserve disk and buffer storage, ensure referential consistency across tables, and prevent data anomalies where modifying or deleting a piece of information corrupts or duplicates related facts.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Avoids data duplication across rows, Prevents Insertion, Deletion, and Modification anomalies, Ensures data dependencies make logical sense. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF)?
questions.answer: Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) is a stricter version of 3NF. A table is in BCNF if it is in 3NF and for every functional dependency X -> Y, X must be a super key. It resolves edge-case anomalies that can occur in 3NF when multiple overlapping candidate keys exist.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Stricter form of 3NF (also called 3.5NF), For every functional dependency X -> Y, X must be a super key, Eliminates anomalies from overlapping candidate keys. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is functional dependency?
questions.answer: A functional dependency (X -> Y) is a relationship between attributes where the value of attribute set X uniquely determines the value of attribute set Y. If two tuples have identical values for X, they must have identical values for Y.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Notation X -> Y (X determines Y), Basis for database normalization, X is determinant, Y is dependent. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is denormalization?
questions.answer: Denormalization is the deliberate process of adding redundant data or grouping normalized tables back together to optimize read query performance and minimize expensive JOIN operations in read-heavy analytical or reporting systems.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Trade-off: read speed vs storage and write consistency, Reduces number of SQL JOINs, Common in Data Warehousing and OLAP systems. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is a database transaction?
questions.answer: A database transaction is a logical unit of work consisting of one or more database operations (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) executed as a single indivisible operation that either completely succeeds (COMMIT) or completely fails (ROLLBACK).
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Logical unit of work, All-or-nothing execution, Guarantees data consistency through ACID properties. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What are ACID properties?
questions.answer: ACID properties are four foundational guarantees that ensure reliable transaction processing in databases: Atomicity (all operations succeed or all roll back), Consistency (transactions preserve DB rules and constraints), Isolation (concurrent transactions execute independently without interference), and Durability (committed changes persist permanently even after system crashes).
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Atomicity: all or nothing, Consistency: valid states and constraint adherence, Isolation: concurrent transactions do not interfere. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is transaction isolation?
questions.answer: Transaction isolation ensures that concurrent transactions execute without reading or overwriting each other's uncommitted modifications, preventing concurrency side effects like dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads through isolation levels and locks.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Prevents concurrent transaction interference, Governed by SQL isolation levels, Implemented via two-phase locking (2PL) or MVCC. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is a dirty read?
questions.answer: A dirty read occurs when Transaction A reads uncommitted data modified by Transaction B. If Transaction B subsequently fails and rolls back, Transaction A has processed data that never officially existed in the database.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Reading uncommitted changes of another transaction, Violates isolation, Occurs at READ UNCOMMITTED isolation level. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is a phantom read?
questions.answer: A phantom read occurs when Transaction A executes a query reading a set of rows matching a WHERE clause, and Transaction B inserts new rows matching that criteria and commits, so when Transaction A runs the identical query again, new 'phantom' rows appear.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies New rows appear in range query on re-execution, Caused by concurrent INSERT operations, Prevented by SERIALIZABLE isolation level or range locks. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is database indexing?
questions.answer: Database indexing is a data structure technique (typically B-Trees or B+ Trees) that allows the database engine to find and retrieve specific rows significantly faster than scanning the entire table sequentially (Full Table Scan), at the cost of additional disk space and slower write operations.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Speeds up search and filter queries, Reduces disk I/O operations from O(N) to O(log N), Trade-off: requires extra storage and slows INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What are the disadvantages of indexing?
questions.answer: The disadvantages of indexing are increased storage consumption on disk and buffer pool memory, and decreased performance for write operations (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) because every index structure must be rebalanced and updated whenever table data changes.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Extra disk and RAM overhead, Slows down write performance (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE), Index maintenance overhead during table bulk loads. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What are clustered and non-clustered indexes?
questions.answer: A clustered index physically sorts and stores the actual table rows on disk in order of the index key; therefore, a table can have only one clustered index (usually on the primary key). A non-clustered index creates a separate inverted structure containing index keys and pointers (row locators) to the physical rows, and a table can have multiple non-clustered indexes.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Clustered: dictates physical row storage, one per table, Non-clustered: separate lookup tree with row pointers, multiple per table, Clustered is faster for range scans. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: Why are B+ Trees used in databases?
questions.answer: B+ Trees are widely used in databases because all data pointers are stored exclusively in the leaf nodes, while internal nodes store only routing keys, allowing high fan-out and shallow tree depth (fewer disk I/O reads). Furthermore, all leaf nodes are linked sequentially in a doubly-linked list, making range queries and sequential scans extremely fast.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Data records only in leaf nodes (high fan-out, shallow tree), Leaf nodes linked in sequential list (fast range scans), Balanced tree guarantees O(log N) search/insert/delete. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is an operating system?
questions.answer: An operating system (OS) is core system software that manages computer hardware, memory, processor execution, and storage, while providing an abstract interface and common system services for application programs.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Manages hardware and software resources, Provides user/application interface via system calls, CPU scheduling, memory, file systems, device management. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is a kernel?
questions.answer: The kernel is the central, core component of the operating system that runs with highest hardware privileges in kernel mode. It has direct access to the CPU, RAM, and hardware devices, controlling all low-level operations like memory management, process scheduling, and interrupt handling.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Core of the operating system, Executes in privileged kernel mode (Ring 0), Manages hardware, memory, processes, interrupts. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is a process?
questions.answer: A process is a program in execution. It represents the basic unit of execution in an operating system, comprising the program code (text section), current activity (program counter, registers), stack (local variables, function calls), and heap (dynamically allocated memory).
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Program loaded into memory and executing, Contains text, data, stack, and heap segments, Managed by the OS via Process Control Block (PCB). Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is a thread?
questions.answer: A thread is the smallest schedulable unit of CPU execution within a process, often called a lightweight process. Multiple threads of the same process share the process's code section, data section, and open files, but each thread has its own Program Counter, registers, and stack.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Smallest unit of CPU dispatch, Lightweight process within a host process, Shares heap, code, and files with sibling threads. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
questions.answer: A process has an isolated, private virtual address space, requiring heavyweight IPC (Inter-Process Communication) and expensive context switches. A thread runs within a process, sharing the same address space and heap, enabling fast, lightweight context switches and direct memory sharing, but a crash in one thread can crash the entire process.
questions.logic: Interviewer expectation: Clarifies Process: separate address space, high context switch cost, Thread: shared address space, low context switch cost, Threads communicate via shared memory; processes via IPC. Answer directly with definition first, followed by internal operation and production trade-offs.

questions.question: Why are threads considered lightweight?
